title: Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO): Anatomy of a Growth Machine
subtitle: Most autopsies begin after a story has ended. This one looks at a company while it is still very much alive.
summary: Broadcom finished FY2025 with US$63.887 billion in revenue, up 23.9%, while net profit rose 292.3%. I look at what drove those results, how much came from tax and accounting effects, and whether the cash backs them up.
content:
Most autopsies begin after a story has ended. On this blog, I’d like to try the opposite: take a look at a company while it is still very much alive, and examine just what makes it tick.

And that brings me to the first company under my coverage: Broadcom.

Broadcom sits at the intersection of three topics that speak to the financial analyst in me: investment in AI infrastructure, the economics of enterprise software and the financial aftermath of large acquisitions.

The thread connecting all three can be framed as one simple question: can Broadcom turn the demand for its technology into stable cash returns? And for you, my readers: will this be a good stock to invest in?

Come along on this post, and the ones that follow, as I attempt to answer this question. But first, let us take a look at Broadcom and what this company actually does.

Broadcom: A Tale of Two Businesses

Broadcom Inc., listed on Nasdaq under AVGO, designs and supplies semiconductor solutions and infrastructure software. Its products serve a broad range of applications: from data centers and wireless devices, to broadband connectivity, industrial equipment and even enterprise computing.

There are two sides to Broadcom worth getting to know. Alongside its semiconductor business sits a substantial infrastructure software operation. The current AI boom helps provide some context on the excitement around the company, but truly gaining a deeper understanding of Broadcom means looking at both.

Its FY2025 revenue gives us a useful starting point:

Semiconductor solutions contributed 57.7% of Broadcom’s FY2025 revenue. This segment of Broadcom’s business supplies custom AI accelerators and networking chips used in data centres, alongside technology for wireless devices, broadband and storage. Those applications help explain where the money comes from: customers buy Broadcom’s technology for the devices and computing infrastructure they are building. Spending on AI infrastructure is therefore one part of the semiconductor business’s wider exposure to investment and production across these markets (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 3-5).

Meanwhile, the other segment of Broadcom’s business, software, contributed the remaining 42.3% of revenue. Here, the company supplies software that enterprises use to run, manage and secure their IT systems (e.g. private-cloud and mainframe environments). The acquisition of VMware in November 2023 expanded this operation, particularly its private-cloud offering (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 5-6, 60). With software accounting for more than two-fifths of revenue, its performance has a substantial bearing on Broadcom’s overall results.

Who buys those products matters too. Broadcom’s five largest end customers accounted for approximately 40% of FY2025 revenue across all sales channels (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 39); leaving a substantial share of sales dependent on the purchasing decisions of just a few customers.

That paints a clearer picture of the driving factors and dependencies behind Broadcom’s revenues. But how do these sales figures translate into profit?

Booming Profits: Under a Microscope

Broadcom finished FY2025, which ended on 2 November 2025, with US$63.887 billion in revenue, up 23.9% from the previous year. Operating profit increased 89.3% to US$25.484 billion, while net profit reached US$23.126 billion (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 48), a rise of 292.3%.

Reported annual results in US$ billions

MetricFY2023FY2024FY2025FY25 Growth
Revenue35.81951.57463.887+23.9%
Gross profit24.69032.50943.294+33.2%
Operating profit16.20713.46325.484+89.3%
Net profit14.0825.89523.126+292.3%

Source: Broadcom Inc. 2025 Annual Report

Higher sales helped, but the cost structure changed too. Gross profit increased by US$10.785 billion, while operating expenses fell by US$1.236 billion. Together, those movements explain the US$12.021 billion increase in operating profit.

As seen in Figure 2, profit growth has outpaced sales growth: Broadcom earned considerably more profit from each dollar of revenue. For every US$100 of sales, US$67.77 remained after cost of revenue in FY2025, compared with US$63.03 a year earlier. After operating expenses, that amount rose from US$26.10 to US$39.89. We can see a substantial improvement in operating profitability before even reaching the tax line. Furthermore, net profit margin climbed even more sharply, from 11.4% to 36.2%.

What caught my eye was the contribution from the software segment. Despite contributing less revenue, it delivered a larger increase in segment operating profit: US$6.788 billion. Broadcom has attributed that improvement to demand for VMware Cloud Foundation, changes in licensing arrangements and lower labour costs following VMware’s integration (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 41). Meanwhile, semiconductor solutions added US$4.473 billion to operating profit, driven mainly by demand for custom AI accelerators and AI networking products.

Together, software and semiconductors contributed US$11.261 billion to the operating-profit increase. A further US$760 million came from lower unallocated expenses: costs such as acquisition-related amortizations and stock-based compensation that Broadcom records outside the two segments (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 41).

Talking about expenses, we can see that selling, general and administrative expenses fell by US$748 million, restructuring and other operating charges declined by US$942 million, and operating-expense amortization dropped by US$1.213 billion. Together, these reductions outweighed a US$1.667 billion increase in research and development expenses, leaving total operating expenses US$1.236 billion lower (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 40). Broadcom therefore earned more gross profit while recording fewer operating expenses overall, a combination that every company wishes for.

Whether that can happen again depends on why those expenses fell. Broadcom says the amortisation reduction mainly arose because certain assets from earlier software acquisitions had become fully amortised (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 40). Put simply, the company had finished recognising those particular acquisition costs over their accounting lives. Their absence can keep future expenses lower, but it cannot reproduce the same savings every year. Something to keep in mind moving forward.

That leaves me with a stronger operating result, but several different reasons behind it. Continued sales growth and further operating efficiencies will matter more to sustaining earnings growth once those accounting reductions are already reflected in the comparison. And there is another reason this year’s net profit rose so sharply: lower interest costs helped, while tax changed from an expense to a benefit (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 41-42). Let’s take a closer look at that.

Examination of Tax

Part of the staggering 292.3% increase in net profit was down to Broadcom moving from a US$3.748 billion tax expense in FY2024 to a US$397 million tax benefit in FY2025 (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 48). That change alone added US$4.145 billion to the year-on-year increase in profit.

Figure 3 puts the tax effect into perspective. Tax accounted for about 24.1% of the US$17.231 billion increase in net profit; meanwhile, the bulk of the increase arose from higher pretax profit, which itself includes the operating improvements, lower interest expenses and changes in other income. This is a promising sign, showing that Broadcom did pull its own weight in improving its business.

However, I’d be cautious about taking this as the be-all-and-end-all to future earnings. The tax comparison could be seen as being particularly favorable: FY2024’s expense was affected by a non-recurring transfer of intellectual-property rights to the United States, while FY2025 benefited from audit settlements, the expiry of time limits on certain tax assessments and tax benefits associated with employee share awards (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 42). My guess is that such circumstances helped boost reported profits.

That distinction becomes clearer when looking at the effective tax rate, which moved from approximately 37.8% to negative 1.7%, an anomaly in and of itself. Furthermore, global minimum-tax rules, particularly in Singapore, are expected to materially affect FY2026 results and cash flows (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 36).

Following the Flow

Having examined what drove Broadcom’s earnings, I want to see whether its cash generation gives me similar grounds for confidence. Operating cash flow (the cash generated through its operating activities) rose 37.9% to US$27.537 billion in FY2025 (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 50). That is encouraging: alongside the improvement in reported profit, the business generated substantially more cash to meet its commitments.

Using Broadcom’s reporting convention, I deduct US$623 million of capital expenditure from operating cash flow to arrive at free cash flow of US$26.914 billion (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 50). This reveals how much operating cash remained after capital purchases, before debt repayments, dividends, buybacks and acquisitions.

As Figure 4 shows, cash generation increased across three reported years. The US$26.914 billion generated in FY2025 represented 42.1% of FY2025 revenue. Put another way, Broadcom generated approximately US$42.13 in free cash flow for every US$100 of sales, compared with US$37.64 a year earlier.

The modest capital expenditure needs some context though. Broadcom outsources most manufacturing, which limits its need to finance production facilities directly (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 8). Its research and development expense, discussed earlier, also sits outside the capital-expenditure figure.

Strong cash generation is encouraging, though I’d also consider what it means for existing shareholders. Broadcom’s operating cash flow includes an add-back of US$7.568 billion for stock-based compensation, an expense recognised in profit without an equivalent cash payment when recorded (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 50). Paying employees in shares helps preserve cash, but issuing additional shares can dilute existing owners’ interests.

Broadcom also spent US$2.450 billion on its repurchase programme and a separate US$3.860 billion repurchasing shares for employee tax withholding. Nevertheless, year-end shares outstanding increased from 4.686 billion to 4.741 billion (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 47, 50).

On balance, the cash-flow figures give me confidence in Broadcom’s ability to fund its business and meet its obligations. I therefore view FY2025 as a stronger year financially, all things being said.

More Room to Breathe

The stronger cash generation mentioned earlier also shows up on the balance sheet. Cash increased from US$9.348 billion to US$16.178 billion, while debt principal fell from US$69.847 billion to US$67.120 billion (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 47, 76). Subtracting cash from debt principal gives net debt of US$50.942 billion, down from US$60.499 billion.

Figure 5 shows that Broadcom improved its position mainly by building up cash. Its cash balance rose by US$6.830 billion, while debt principal fell by US$2.727 billion. That matters as the company has more resources available to meet repayments or withstand a weaker year, although its borrowings remain substantial. Regardless, this is still meaningful progress in its ability to manage debt.

The repayment figures do invite some scrutiny. Broadcom repaid US$18.478 billion during FY2025, but also raised US$15.666 billion through borrowing (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 50). The resulting net cash repayment was US$2.812 billion. Looking only at the gross repayments would give an exaggerated impression of how quickly the company was reducing debt.

The ratios provide another way to assess the change:

Selected financial ratios

Financial ratioFY2024FY2025
Current ratio1.17×1.71×
Debt-to-equity ratio1.00×0.80×
Interest coverage3.41×7.94×

The current ratio means Broadcom had approximately US$1.71 of current assets for every US$1 of current liabilities, compared with US$1.17 a year earlier. Some of those assets still need to be collected or converted into cash, but the increased coverage is reassuring. Operating profit also reached 7.94 times interest expense, providing a larger earnings cushion against that charge.

For debt-to-equity, I use the debt recorded on the balance sheet: US$65.136 billion in FY2025, compared with US$67.566 billion in FY2024. This differs from the principal amounts in Figure 5 because the accounting balances reflect adjustments including unamortised discounts and issuance costs (Broadcom Inc., 2025, pp. 47, 76). Lower recorded debt and higher equity both contributed to the ratio’s improvement.

There was also room to fund dividends. Cash dividend payments totalled US$11.142 billion (Broadcom Inc., 2025, p. 50), absorbing approximately 41.4% of Broadcom-reported free cash flow. That measure covered the payment about 2.42 times. The dividend therefore left a substantial amount for debt repayments, repurchases and other investments, giving management choices over how to use the remaining cash.

My assessment is that Broadcom ended FY2025 better equipped to handle its financial commitments. The combination of more cash, lower debt and stronger interest coverage gives it greater resilience if conditions become less favourable, and more flexibility to pursue growth.

So… What’s the Autopsy Result?

The verdict is… positive! Broadcom ended FY2025 financially stronger, with improved profitability, greater cash generation and more room to manage its debt. The tax uplift and lower acquisition-related charges warrant caution when projecting further growth, but the underlying progress is convincing. Whether that makes the shares worth buying comes down to valuation. Follow along on my next post for more!

All amounts in US$ millions unless stated

MeasureCalculation and result

Net-profit bridge5,895 + (22,729 − 9,916) + (3,748 − (−397)) + 273 = 23,126. Tax share of increase: 4,145 / 17,231 = 24.1%.

Free cash flowOperating cash flow − capital expenditure. FY2023: 18,085 − 452 = 17,633; FY2024: 19,962 − 548 = 19,414; FY2025: 27,537 − 623 = 26,914.
FCF margin and dividend coverFY2025 FCF margin: 26,914 / 63,887 = 42.1%. Dividend payout: 11,142 / 26,914 = 41.4%. Cover: 26,914 / 11,142 = 2.42 times.
